newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bunds lose some shine, but outlook still golden.
newsitem.headline: Bunds lose some shine, but outlook still golden.

text.p: Bund futures continued to benefit from stronger Treasuries on Wednesday, raising expectations that the market has resumed its upward course of late last year.

The DTB Bund futures contract spent much of the day trading at strongly higher levels on Wednesday, but fell late in the afternoon to drift only a couple of basis points above the 101.24 close on Tuesday.
Despite the day's swings, analysts were unswayed in their new more optimistic mood about Bunds. "This market should go higher," said Stuart Trow, analyst at Norinchukin Int'l Plc.

He and others said that with the U.S. debt market showing some strength, the major obstacle to further Bund gains had been removed, allowing investors to focus on bond market-friendly German economic fundamentals.
Many now look for the futures contract to trend toward the 102.07 high of December 3 and do not even rule out a breach of that level.
The contract first faces trendline resistance at around 101.55 based on a resistance line drawn from the January 6 low when the contract stood at 99.56.
But traders expected that level to be broken as soon as Friday when a slew of U.S. data are scheduled for release including trade, capacity utilisation and industrial production data.
Much of the market's strength, however, has been centered in the futures market and investor demand for cash bonds has remained subdued.
One factor putting investors off is the spread between Bunds and Treasuries, which at 87 basis points is near its highest level since 1990.
Some believe that spread could widen out to near 100 basis points before starting to narrow back in again.

The German yield curve, meanwhile, flattend by two basis points on the day with the spread between two- and 10-year notes narrowing to 245 basis points. Much of that flattening took place in the two- to five-year area with the curve between five- and 10-years showing no change.
Word early in the day that averaged pan-German consumer prices were 1.5 percent in 1996 had little impact on the Bund market as the figure had already been expected.
